specStatements.text: Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 × 10^-10 metres.
The basic structure of an atom is a positively charged nucleus composed of both protons and neutrons surrounded by negatively charged electrons.
The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom. Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

The electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus (different energy levels). The electron arrangements may change with the absorption of electromagnetic radiation (move further from the nucleus; a higher energy level) or by the emission of electromagnetic radiation (move closer to the nucleus; a lower energy level).
In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. Atoms have no overall electrical charge.
All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons. The number of protons in an atom of an element is called its atomic number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom is called its mass number.
Atoms can be represented as shown in this example:
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electron (s).
Students should be able to relate differences between isotopes to differences in conventional representations of their identities, charges and masses.
New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom. The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

The results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged. This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Students should be able to describe:
• why the new evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model
• the difference between the plum pudding model of the atom and the nuclear model of the atom.
Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Bohr is treated exactly as far as the specification takes him: he adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations. Nothing here asks about emission or absorption spectra, spectral line series, apparatus, or any derivation of allowed orbits, and no question requires a student to name or describe an experiment that supported Bohr's model.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Chadwick appears only as the specification states: his experimental work provided the evidence showing that neutrons exist within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea. No apparatus, no target materials, no measurements and no reasoning from his experiment are taught or examined here; questions ask only what his work provided evidence for and when it happened relative to the acceptance of the nucleus.

concepts.definition: The particle that all matter is built from. Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 × 10^-10 metres, so about ten million atoms would fit side by side across a millimetre.
The positively charged centre of an atom, composed of both protons and neutrons. It is far smaller than the atom but contains most of the atom's mass.
A positively charged particle found in the nucleus of an atom. The number of protons determines which element the atom is.
An uncharged particle found in the nucleus of an atom alongside the protons. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons.
A negatively charged particle that surrounds the nucleus of an atom. Electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus and have a very small mass compared with a proton or a neutron.

The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom. Since an atomic radius is about 1 × 10^-10 m, a nuclear radius is of the order of 1 × 10^-14 m or smaller, so almost all of an atom is empty space.
One of the different distances from the nucleus at which the electrons in an atom are arranged. An electron further from the nucleus is in a higher energy level.

concepts.term: Absorption of electromagnetic radiation by an atom
concepts.definition: An electron arrangement may change when the atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation: an electron moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.

concepts.term: Emission of electromagnetic radiation by an atom
concepts.definition: An electron arrangement may change by the emission of electromagnetic radiation: an electron moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level.
In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus, so the positive and negative charges balance and atoms have no overall electrical charge.
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons, so the atomic number identifies the element.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
An atom is written as its chemical symbol with the mass number above the atomic number to the left of it, for example ²³₁₁Na: mass number 23 at the top, atomic number 11 below.
Because the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons, the number of neutrons in an atom is the mass number minus the atomic number. For ²³₁₁Na this gives 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons.
Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
An atom that has lost one or more outer electrons. It then has more protons than electrons, so it carries an overall positive charge.

Two representations show isotopes of the same element when the lower number (atomic number) and the chemical symbol match but the upper number (mass number) differs, as in ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl. A difference in charge is shown by a + or - sign after the symbol and makes the particle an ion, not a different isotope.
A description of a system used to explain observations and make predictions. New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The model that followed the discovery of the electron. It suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged. Most alpha particles passed through, but a small number were deflected through large angles, which the plum pudding model could not explain.
The model in which an atom's mass is concentrated in a charged nucleus at the centre, with electrons around it. This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.

concepts.term: Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model
concepts.definition: Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.

misconceptions.question: How big is the nucleus compared with the whole atom?
misconceptions.correct: The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom, so almost all of the atom is empty space.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus is a bit smaller than the atom, but it fills a good part of the middle - an atom is basically solid all the way through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook and exam diagrams have to draw the nucleus large enough to see, so it is often shown as perhaps a tenth of the atom's width. Students read the picture as if it were to scale.
misconceptions.correction: A scale drawing is impossible on paper: if an atom were drawn 1 metre across, the nucleus would be smaller than a tenth of a millimetre. The specification fixes the ratio - the nuclear radius is less than 1/10 000 of the atomic radius.

misconceptions.question: Which particles account for most of the mass of an atom?
misconceptions.correct: Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus, in the protons and neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: There are as many electrons as protons, so the electrons must supply a fair share of the atom's mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting arguments feel like mass arguments: equal numbers of two kinds of particle suggests equal contributions. The relative mass of an electron is rarely quoted in physics lessons at this stage.
misconceptions.correction: Number and mass are different things. The specification states that most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus; an electron's mass is negligible beside that of a proton or a neutron.

misconceptions.question: An atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. Where does the electron move to?
misconceptions.correct: It moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.
misconceptions.misconception: Absorbing radiation pulls the electron in towards the nucleus, because the atom is taking something in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of 'absorb' is 'draw inwards', so students map the direction of the radiation onto the direction the electron moves.
misconceptions.correction: Absorption gives the electron energy, and having more energy means being further from the nucleus - a higher energy level. Emission is the reverse: the electron moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level.

misconceptions.question: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?
misconceptions.correct: In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus, so the charges cancel.
misconceptions.misconception: The atom's charged particles are locked away inside it, so the charge cannot be felt from outside and the atom counts as neutral.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students explain neutrality by hiding the charge rather than balancing it, especially since the protons really are inside the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: Neutrality comes from equal numbers, not from concealment. Equal numbers of protons and electrons mean equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so the atom has no overall electrical charge.

misconceptions.question: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom of that element.
misconceptions.misconception: The atomic number is the number of neutrons, since the mass number already counts the protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students try to make the two numbers count separate things, so they assign one number to protons and the other to neutrons.
misconceptions.correction: The atomic number counts protons only; the mass number counts protons and neutrons together. Neutrons are never given their own number - you find them by subtracting.

misconceptions.question: What does the mass number of an atom tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number is the number of neutrons, because neutrons are the particles that add mass without adding charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutrons are introduced as the particles that change the mass of an isotope, so students attach the word 'mass' to neutrons alone.
misconceptions.correction: The mass number is the total of protons and neutrons. Changing the neutron number does change the mass number, but the protons are counted in it too.

misconceptions.question: What is different between two isotopes of the same element?
misconceptions.correct: Isotopes of an element have different numbers of neutrons but the same number of protons.
misconceptions.misconception: Isotopes have different numbers of protons - that is what makes them different versions of the atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Protons are the particle students think about first, so any difference between two atoms gets attributed to them.
misconceptions.correction: All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons; if the proton number changed, it would be a different element. Isotopes differ only in neutron number, and therefore in mass number.

misconceptions.question: Do isotopes of an element have different charges?
misconceptions.correct: No. Isotopes are still atoms, so they have no overall electrical charge; they differ in mass number only.
misconceptions.misconception: An isotope is an atom that has been changed, so it must carry a charge like an ion does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Isotope' and 'ion' are both introduced as 'an atom that is not the ordinary one', and both are shown with extra numbers or signs written round the symbol.
misconceptions.correction: The two ideas are separate. An isotope differs in neutrons, shown by a different mass number. An ion differs in electrons, shown by a + or - sign after the symbol. ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl are isotopes; ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁵₁₇Cl⁻ are not.

misconceptions.question: How does an atom become a positive ion?
misconceptions.correct: Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electron(s).
misconceptions.misconception: The atom gains a proton, because to become more positive you have to add positive charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More positive' is read as 'more positive charge added', and protons are the positive particle students name first.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus is not changed by ordinary ionisation - adding a proton would make it a different element altogether. Removing a negative electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the particle is positive.

misconceptions.question: What did the plum pudding model say the atom was like?
misconceptions.correct: The atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
misconceptions.misconception: The plum pudding model had a small positive nucleus in the middle, with the electrons going round it like currants around a centre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name suggests fruit spread around a body, and students already know the nuclear picture, so they read the nucleus back into the earlier model.
misconceptions.correction: The plum pudding model had no nucleus at all: the positive charge was spread through the whole atom, with the electrons stuck inside it. Concentrating charge and mass into a nucleus was exactly what the alpha particle scattering results forced scientists to do.

misconceptions.question: What conclusion came from the alpha particle scattering experiment?
misconceptions.correct: The mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and the nucleus was charged.
misconceptions.misconception: The scattering experiment proved that the electrons orbit the nucleus at set distances in energy levels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The scattering experiment and Bohr's orbits are taught minutes apart and both belong to the 'modern' picture, so students merge the evidence with the later refinement.
misconceptions.correction: The scattering results say nothing about electrons. They lead to a concentrated, charged nucleus. Specific electron orbits came later, when Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model.

misconceptions.question: What happened to the alpha particles fired at the foil?
misconceptions.correct: Most passed straight through; only a small number were deflected through large angles.
misconceptions.misconception: Most of the alpha particles bounced back off the foil - that is how they knew there was something solid there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The dramatic part of the story is the rebound, so it is the part students remember, and the word 'scattering' sounds as though everything was scattered.
misconceptions.correction: The rarity of the large deflections is the whole argument. If almost everything passes through, the atom must be mostly empty space; because a few come back, the thing that turns them must be tiny, massive and charged.

misconceptions.question: What was Niels Bohr's contribution to the model of the atom?
misconceptions.correct: Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.
misconceptions.misconception: Bohr discovered the nucleus and built the first nuclear model of the atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'Bohr model' is the diagram students draw most often, so his name gets attached to the whole nuclear picture rather than to the one change he made to it.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus came from the alpha particle scattering results. Bohr's contribution was to adapt that existing nuclear model by placing the electrons at specific distances.

misconceptions.question: When was the evidence for neutrons in the nucleus obtained?
misconceptions.correct: Chadwick's experimental work provided the evidence about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
misconceptions.misconception: Protons and neutrons were found together, as soon as scientists knew there was a nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Protons and neutrons are always drawn and listed together as 'the nuclear particles', which hides the long gap between the two discoveries.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus was accepted first, then its positive charge was shown to be made of protons. Only about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for neutrons.

misconceptions.question: What makes scientists change or replace a model?
misconceptions.correct: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
misconceptions.misconception: Models change when enough scientists change their minds, or when someone influential prefers a different idea.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that science 'moves on' and that famous names are attached to models, so the process looks like fashion or authority rather than evidence.
misconceptions.correction: It is the evidence that decides. A model survives while it explains what is observed; when experiments produce results the model cannot account for, the model is changed or replaced.

misconceptions.question: In ²³₁₁Na, what does each number tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The upper number, 23, is the mass number; the lower number, 11, is the atomic number.
misconceptions.misconception: The top number is the atomic number, because the atomic number is the more important one so it goes first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reading order puts the top number first, and the atomic number is the number quoted first in lessons, so the two 'firsts' get matched up.
misconceptions.correction: The larger number on top is the mass number (protons + neutrons); the smaller number underneath is the atomic number (protons only). Checking which is larger is a quick way to see if you have them the right way round.

misconceptions.question: What is the radius of an atom?
misconceptions.correct: Atoms have a radius of about 1 × 10^-10 metres.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom is about 1 × 10^-10 mm across - it is tiny, so the smallest unit on the ruler must be the one to use.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the digits of the standard figure but not its unit, and reach for millimetres because that is the smallest length they meet in the laboratory.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives the figure in metres: about 1 × 10^-10 m. Quoting it in millimetres shrinks the atom by a further factor of a thousand, taking it well below the size of a nucleus.

misconceptions.question: Where are the electrons in an atom?
misconceptions.correct: The electrons surround the nucleus, arranged at different distances from it.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons are in the nucleus too, mixed in with the protons and neutrons - that is where all the particles are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'The atom is made of protons, neutrons and electrons' is often said in one breath, and diagrams that crowd the particles together reinforce it.
misconceptions.correction: Only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus. The negatively charged electrons are outside it, at different distances from the nucleus in different energy levels.

misconceptions.question: What is the charge on the nucleus of an atom?
misconceptions.correct: The nucleus is positively charged, because it contains protons and neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus must be negative - opposites attract, and it is the nucleus that attracts the electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Opposites attract' is remembered without tracking which particle carries which sign, so the rule gets applied to the wrong end of the pair.
misconceptions.correction: The electrons are the negative particles; the nucleus is the positive one, and that is why the two attract. The specification states the structure precisely: a positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons.

misconceptions.question: What was the model of the atom before the electron was discovered?
misconceptions.correct: Atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists always knew atoms contained smaller bits inside them - the plum pudding picture was there from the start.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet the sub-atomic particles first and the history second, so it is hard to imagine a time when 'atom' really meant a single indivisible object.
misconceptions.correction: The order matters. First the indivisible sphere; then the discovery of the electron, which led to the plum pudding model; then the scattering results, which led to the nuclear model.

misconceptions.question: How was it established that nuclear charge is made of protons?
misconceptions.correct: Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge; these were named protons.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus is a single lump of positive charge; the word 'proton' is just another name for the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: For hydrogen the nucleus really is one proton, and diagrams of the scattering experiment show the nucleus as one solid blob of positive charge.
misconceptions.correction: The scattering results showed only that the nucleus was charged. Later experiments showed that this charge divides into a whole number of identical positive particles, and the name proton was given to those particles.

misconceptions.question: What happens to an electron when an atom emits electromagnetic radiation?
misconceptions.correct: The electron moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level.
misconceptions.misconception: The electron must leave the atom - something has to be given out, and the electron is what is given out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Emission is understood as 'the atom loses something', and the electron is the particle students think of as loose enough to go.
misconceptions.correction: What is emitted is electromagnetic radiation, not the electron. The electron stays in the atom and simply moves closer to the nucleus, into a lower energy level.

misconceptions.question: What part do neutrons play in the charge of an atom?
misconceptions.correct: None. Neutrons are uncharged; the atom is neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
misconceptions.misconception: The neutrons cancel out the charge on the protons, which is what makes the atom neutral.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'neutron' sounds like the cause of 'neutral', so students give the neutron an active cancelling role rather than no charge at all.
misconceptions.correction: A neutron has no charge, so it cannot cancel anything. Neutrality comes from the balance between protons in the nucleus and electrons around it.

misconceptions.question: Does an atom gain or lose electrons to become a positive ion?
misconceptions.correct: It loses one or more outer electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Gaining electrons makes it positive, because you are adding particles and adding always makes something bigger or more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Gain' is associated with 'plus' and 'more', and the sign of the electron's own charge is not tracked through the reasoning.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons are negative, so gaining them makes an ion more negative. Losing outer electrons leaves an excess of protons, giving a positive ion, which is what the specification states.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a scientific model that gets replaced?
misconceptions.correct: It is changed or replaced because new experimental evidence cannot be explained by it; the earlier model was still a reasonable account of the evidence available at the time.
misconceptions.misconception: The old model was simply wrong and worthless, and scientists were foolish to hold it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The history is presented as a sequence of corrections, so each earlier model looks like a mistake rather than the best fit to the evidence then available.
misconceptions.correction: The plum pudding model explained what was known when it was proposed. It was replaced only when the scattering results produced evidence it could not account for - that is how models are supposed to work.

mcqs.stem: Which value is closest to the radius of an atom?

options.rationale: The specification states that atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 × 10^-10 metres.
The digits are remembered but the unit is not; a student reaching for the smallest unit on a ruler writes mm and shrinks the atom by a factor of a thousand.
This is the order of a nuclear radius. A student who does not separate the size of the nucleus from the size of the atom recalls the wrong one of the two figures.
A millimetre. Chosen by students who equate 'very small' with the smallest length they can actually see marked on laboratory equipment.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the basic structure of an atom?

options.text: A positive nucleus of protons, neutrons and electrons, held in a shell
options.rationale: Students who learn the three particles as one list place all three in the nucleus, keeping the charge correct but the position wrong.

options.text: A positive nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negative electrons
options.rationale: This is the structure the specification gives: a positively charged nucleus composed of both protons and neutrons surrounded by negatively charged electrons.

options.text: A negative nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by positive electrons
options.rationale: The signs are swapped by a student who applies 'opposites attract' to the wrong particle and makes the attracting centre negative.

options.text: A neutral nucleus of neutrons, surrounded by protons and electrons
options.rationale: Attractive to students who tie 'neutron' to 'nucleus' by name and then push both charged particles outside it.

mcqs.stem: An atom has a radius of 1 × 10^-10 m. Which value could be the radius of its nucleus?

options.rationale: A tenth of the atomic radius - the ratio suggested by a typical textbook diagram rather than by the specification.
The correct figure written in the wrong unit by a student who does not keep track of metres and millimetres.
A nuclear radius is less than 1/10 000 of the atomic radius, so it must be smaller than 1 × 10^-14 m. Only this value satisfies that.
The atomic radius itself, chosen by students who treat the nucleus and the atom as effectively the same object.

mcqs.stem: Where is almost all of the mass of an atom found?

options.text: In the electrons, because there are as many electrons as there are protons
options.rationale: Equal numbers are read as equal contributions to mass by students who have never compared the particles' masses.

options.text: In the space around the nucleus, because that is where most volume is
options.rationale: Volume is confused with mass; the region that takes up most room is assumed to hold most of the matter.

options.text: Spread evenly through the atom, because the particles are evenly mixed
options.rationale: A leftover from the plum pudding picture, in which everything is distributed uniformly through the atom.

options.text: In the nucleus, because protons and neutrons are far heavier than electrons
options.rationale: The specification states that most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: How are the electrons in an atom arranged?

options.text: At different distances from the nucleus, in different energy levels
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states about the arrangement of electrons.

options.text: Inside the nucleus, mixed in among the protons and the neutrons
options.rationale: Chosen by students who list all three particles as being 'in the atom's centre'.

options.text: Packed tightly around the nucleus so that the atom is solid
options.rationale: Fits the belief that an atom is a solid object throughout rather than mostly empty space.

options.text: Fixed in place, all at the same distance from the nucleus
options.rationale: A simplified single-ring diagram is remembered, losing the idea of different distances and different energy levels.

mcqs.stem: An atom emits electromagnetic radiation. What happens to one of its electrons?

options.text: It moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
options.rationale: The absorption case is given instead; students who do not link energy to distance reverse the two.

options.text: It moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
options.rationale: The specification pairs emission of electromagnetic radiation with an electron moving closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level.

options.text: It leaves the atom, so the atom becomes a positive ion
options.rationale: 'Emit' is read as the atom giving out a particle, and the electron is the particle students expect to go.

options.text: It moves into the nucleus and joins the protons there
options.rationale: Moving closer is taken to its extreme by students who already picture electrons as belonging in the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?

options.text: Its charged particles are all held inside the nucleus together
options.rationale: Neutrality is explained by hiding the charge rather than balancing it - and it also misplaces the electrons.

options.text: The neutrons in the nucleus cancel out the charge on the protons
options.rationale: 'Neutron' is heard as the cause of 'neutral', giving the uncharged particle an active cancelling role.

options.text: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons, whose charges cancel
options.rationale: The specification states that in an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons, so atoms have no overall electrical charge.

options.text: Its electrons move so fast that their charge averages out to zero
options.rationale: Motion is offered as the reason for neutrality, a plausible-sounding idea for students who picture electrons whizzing round.

mcqs.stem: What is the atomic number of an element?

options.text: The number of neutrons in an atom of that element
options.rationale: Students try to give each of the two numbers its own particle, so one is assigned to neutrons.

options.text: The total number of protons and neutrons in the atom
options.rationale: This is the mass number; the two definitions are commonly swapped.

options.text: The number of energy levels filled with electrons
options.rationale: Chosen by students who associate the number written with the symbol with the shell diagram they have drawn.

options.text: The number of protons in an atom of that element
options.rationale: The specification defines the atomic number as the number of protons in an atom of an element.

mcqs.stem: What is the mass number of an atom?

options.text: The total number of protons and neutrons in the atom
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of mass number.

options.text: The number of neutrons that the atom's nucleus holds
options.rationale: Neutrons are introduced as the particles that change an isotope's mass, so 'mass' is attached to them alone.

options.text: The total number of protons, neutrons and electrons
options.rationale: A student who thinks electrons contribute appreciable mass counts them in as well.

options.text: The mass of a single atom of the element in grams
options.rationale: The word 'mass' is taken literally as a measured mass rather than as a count of nuclear particles.

mcqs.stem: An atom is represented as ²³₁₁Na. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?

options.rationale: A student who believes the lower number counts neutrons reads the answer straight off the symbol.
The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, so neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12.
The mass number is taken to be the neutron count, so no subtraction is done at all.
The two numbers are added instead of subtracted, a common slip when the relationship between them is not understood.

mcqs.stem: An atom is represented as ⁴⁰₁₈Ar. What does the number 40 tell you?

options.text: The atomic number: the number of protons in the nucleus
options.rationale: The number read first is assumed to be the atomic number, because that is the term met first in lessons.

options.text: The number of neutrons that the nucleus of the atom holds
options.rationale: Follows directly from believing the mass number counts neutrons only.

options.text: The mass number: the total number of protons and neutrons
options.rationale: In the conventional representation the upper number is the mass number, the total of protons and neutrons.

options.text: The number of electrons arranged in the energy levels
options.rationale: Attractive because the electron number does equal one of the two numbers shown - but it equals the lower one, 18.

mcqs.stem: What are isotopes?

options.text: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of protons
options.rationale: Any difference between two atoms is attributed to protons, the particle students think of first.

options.text: Atoms of an element that have gained or lost some electrons
options.rationale: This defines an ion. 'Isotope' and 'ion' are both learned as 'an altered atom' and get merged.

options.text: Atoms of different elements that have the same mass number
options.rationale: The correct feature (mass number) is kept but attached to the wrong condition, so different elements are allowed.

options.text: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of isotopes.

mcqs.stem: Which pair are isotopes of the same element?

options.text: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl
options.rationale: Same atomic number and symbol, different mass numbers - the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

options.text: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca
options.rationale: The proton numbers differ, so these are different elements; students who think isotopes differ in protons pick this.

options.text: ²³₁₁Na and ²³₁₁Na⁺
options.rationale: These differ in charge, not in neutrons - an atom and its ion, chosen by students who confuse isotopes with ions.

options.text: ⁶⁴₂₉Cu and ⁶⁵₃₀Zn
options.rationale: The mass numbers differ by one, which looks like the isotope pattern until the atomic numbers are checked.

mcqs.stem: Two isotopes of the same element are compared. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They have the same mass number but different atomic numbers
options.rationale: The two numbers are swapped by students who think it is the proton number that varies between isotopes.

options.text: They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers
options.rationale: Isotopes differ in neutron number only, so the proton count and therefore the atomic number is unchanged while the mass number differs.

options.text: They have the same mass number but different overall charges
options.rationale: Describes an atom and its ion; isotopes are neutral atoms and differ in mass, not charge.

options.text: They have different numbers of protons and of neutrons too
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume that a change in mass number requires both nuclear particles to change.

mcqs.stem: How does an atom turn into a positive ion?

options.text: It gains one or more protons in its nucleus
options.rationale: 'More positive' is read as 'add positive charge', so a proton is added - which would change the element entirely.

options.text: It gains one or more of its outer electrons
options.rationale: 'Gain' is associated with 'plus', without tracking that the electron's own charge is negative.

options.text: It loses one or more of its outer electrons
options.rationale: The specification states that atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electron(s).

options.text: It loses one or more neutrons from its nucleus
options.rationale: Losing a particle is the right idea but the wrong particle; removing a neutron changes mass, not charge.

mcqs.stem: What leads scientists to change or replace a model of the atom?

options.text: Enough well-known scientists deciding that they prefer a new idea
options.rationale: Model change is read as a matter of opinion or authority, since models carry famous names.

options.text: The older model being shown to have been worthless all along
options.rationale: Replaced models are assumed to have been simply wrong, rather than the best fit to the evidence of their time.

options.text: A newer model being simpler and easier for students to picture
options.rationale: Simplicity is a real virtue in models, so it is plausible - but it is not what the specification identifies as the driver of change.

options.text: New experimental evidence that the existing model cannot explain
options.rationale: The specification states that new experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.

mcqs.stem: Before the discovery of the electron, what were atoms thought to be?

options.text: Tiny spheres that could not be divided into anything smaller
options.rationale: This is the model the specification describes as preceding the discovery of the electron.

options.text: Tiny spheres of positive charge with electrons stuck inside them
options.rationale: The plum pudding model is placed too early; it could only follow the discovery of the electron.

options.text: Tiny spheres with a nucleus at the centre and orbiting electrons
options.rationale: The familiar modern diagram is read back into the earliest model.

options.text: Tiny spheres made of protons and neutrons packed tightly together
options.rationale: Students assume the nuclear particles were always part of the picture, though both were identified much later.

mcqs.stem: What did the plum pudding model suggest about the atom?

options.text: It has a small positive nucleus with negative electrons orbiting it
options.rationale: The nuclear model is given instead; students read the 'pudding' as a central body with currants around it.

options.text: It is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of the plum pudding model.

options.text: It is a ball of negative charge with positive protons embedded in it
options.rationale: The right shape with the signs reversed, chosen by students who do not track which particle is negative.

options.text: It is a solid sphere that cannot be divided into smaller particles
options.rationale: The model that came before the electron was discovered, not the one the electron's discovery led to.

mcqs.stem: What conclusion did the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment lead to?

options.text: The electrons of an atom orbit the nucleus at particular fixed distances
options.rationale: Bohr's later adaptation is credited to the scattering results, which say nothing about electrons.

options.text: The atom is a solid ball of matter with its charge spread throughout it
options.rationale: This is the model the results overturned; it is chosen by students who miss that most particles passed through.

options.text: The mass of an atom is concentrated in a charged nucleus at the centre
options.rationale: The specification states that the results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged.

options.text: The nucleus contains uncharged neutrons as well as positive protons
options.rationale: Neutrons are assumed to be part of the picture from the start, though the evidence for them came about 20 years later.

mcqs.stem: Which result of the alpha particle scattering experiment could the plum pudding model not explain?

options.text: Almost all of the alpha particles bounced straight back off the foil
options.rationale: The dramatic rebound is remembered as the usual outcome rather than the rare one, which destroys the argument.

options.text: The alpha particles were absorbed by the atoms in the gold foil
options.rationale: Expected by students who picture the atom as solid throughout, so nothing could get through the foil.

options.text: Almost all of the alpha particles passed straight through the foil
options.rationale: A genuine observation, but not the awkward one: a diffuse plum pudding atom would let fast particles through anyway.

options.text: A small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles
options.rationale: A diffuse ball of charge could not turn a fast, massive alpha particle through a large angle; only a tiny, massive, charged nucleus can.

mcqs.stem: What is the key difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?

options.text: In the nuclear model the positive charge and mass sit in a tiny nucleus
options.rationale: The plum pudding model spread positive charge through the whole atom; the nuclear model concentrates charge and mass at the centre.

options.text: In the plum pudding model the electrons orbit a small central nucleus
options.rationale: A nucleus is given to the earlier model, which removes the very difference the question asks about.

options.text: In the nuclear model the centre of the atom carries negative charge
options.rationale: The nucleus is made negative by students who assign the sign to the attracting particle.

options.text: In the nuclear model the electrons hold nearly all of the atom's mass
options.rationale: Mass is placed with the electrons, when the point of the nuclear model is that mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model of the atom?

options.text: The atom has a small central nucleus that holds its mass
options.rationale: The nuclear model itself is credited to Bohr, though it came from the alpha particle scattering results.

options.text: Electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances from it
options.rationale: The specification states that Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and that his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.

options.text: The nucleus of an atom contains neutrons as well as protons
options.rationale: The neutron is attached to the wrong scientist; the evidence for it came from Chadwick's experimental work.

options.text: The positive charge of a nucleus is made of separate protons
options.rationale: The subdivision of nuclear charge came from later experiments, not from Bohr's adaptation of the model.

mcqs.stem: What did later experiments show about the positive charge of any nucleus?

options.text: It comes from one indivisible particle sitting at the centre of the atom
options.rationale: The nucleus is treated as a single lump of charge, which is true only for hydrogen.

options.text: It is produced by the neutrons that James Chadwick later discovered
options.rationale: Charge is attributed to the neutron, and the order of the two discoveries is reversed.

options.text: It can be subdivided into a whole number of identical positive particles
options.rationale: The specification states that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge; these were named protons.

options.text: It is cancelled out by the neutrons that sit alongside in the nucleus
options.rationale: 'Neutron' is heard as a cancelling particle rather than an uncharged one.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the evidence for neutrons is correct?

options.text: It came from the same experiments that first showed that the nucleus exists
options.rationale: Protons and neutrons are always listed together, hiding the long gap between the two discoveries.

options.text: It came from Bohr's calculations of where the electrons must be orbiting
options.rationale: Bohr's name is attached to every part of the modern model rather than to the one change he made.

options.text: It showed that neutrons lie outside the nucleus, among the electrons
options.rationale: Chosen by students who are unsure which particles belong inside the nucleus and which do not.

options.text: It came from Chadwick's work, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted
options.rationale: The specification states that the experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
